content.content:
# The report and the record

## What every report holds

Your brief says where your report goes: a file that it names, your final message, or both. If it names no file, your report is your final message.

A finding is something that your work learned about the tree or the language, and that the record does not hold yet. Examples: a defect, a behaviour that departs from the specification or from a decision of the curator, a measurement. What you did along the way is not a finding, for example the files that you read or edited. Your transcript keeps that.

A fact is a finding that is an established property of the tree, the language, the library or their tools, and that later work builds on. A defect also gets its ledger row, and a fact about it may cite the row.

A point to report is a kind of change or finding that the curator wants to review. Your brief names its points to report. Examples: a changed line of a test that the team wrote, a checker edit inside a change to the library, a changed line of the model program.

Put each of these that you have in your report, in this form, whatever else your brief asks for:

- **Defects.** Each defect that you measured, and the test or ledger row that records it (`tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded").
- **Sentences of the specification made false.** Each sentence of the specification that your change makes false, quoted with its file and line. Such a sentence says what walk or the compiled path does. It is in the effect of an Appendix I entry (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex`), or in a `\revision` or `\note{}` box beside a passage.
- **Decisions.** Each choice that you made among alternatives, as a decision apart from the findings: what you chose, the alternatives, and the evidence, cited. If no decision of the curator covers it, say so, and say which reading you acted on. A decision left as a line inside the findings counts as not made.
- **Points to report.** Each point that your brief names and the work reached, with its evidence, also one that only part of the work reached.
- **For FACTS.** Each fact that your work established, in the hand-over form of "Writing to the record". If your brief let you write FACTS, give instead the number of each entry that you added or rewrote. If your work established no fact, write "none".
- **Commands.** Each command that you had to work out because this skill does not give it, with what it does.
- **Questions for the curator.** If something needs the curator's decision, list it as a decision not taken, in the form that `exploring.md` gives. The reader of your report brings it to the curator. Do not choose which of your items anyone reviews.

## At a point to report

- If the work reaches a point to report, do what the brief says for it. For example, a brief can say that a defect in the code is recorded in a ledger row and not repaired.
- Then finish the work.
- If a step cannot be undone, or would change a decision of the curator, report it instead. List it as a decision not taken, with its alternatives.

## Timings and citations

- If you take a timing that you will keep, run nothing else beside it. All agents of the session share the machine's cores (the `cloud-container` skill).
- Name the machine with every timing: `nproc`, the CPU's model and MHz, the load at start, the JDK, `FORTRESS_THREADS`. Only a pair of timings taken in one run measures a difference.
- If you take a measurement again because the code changed, say what changed.
- In a report, cite the tree at file:line, and quote results, two to five lines, each with its command. Never cite a file under `tmp/`.

## POSITIONS and FACTS

POSITIONS and FACTS describe the present: no dates, no names of who found what, no "corrected" or "superseded" notes. The history of each entry is in `POSITIONS-history.md` and `FACTS-history.md`, beside them. When your work needs the detail of an entry, print the report section that it cites (`$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'`, below). Read its history only when the tree disagrees with the entry.

Each entry is one line that starts with its permanent number: `F-87` in FACTS, `P-48` in POSITIONS. A FACTS entry is the fact as it stands now, what it means for the work, and the test that fails if the fact stops holding, under a bold title. If no test checks the fact, the entry gives the command and the output that show it. It points to the report section that holds the detail. Cite an entry by its number. If the reader must know what the entry says without printing it, add the first words of its title in quotes: F-87, "The first words ...".

## The gap ledger

The ledger's rows are the bug reports that the work fixes. A fix of a row starts with its reproduction, written as a test (`tests-writing.md`).

A row is one line of eight cells, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of a topic section. Reports cite a row by its number, which it keeps for good. A new issue gets a new row.

- Its status is one of seven words: `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`, `CONTESTED`, `RETIRED`, `FIXED`, `DUPLICATE`. The last three close a row. The row template (below) defines each.
- Its class is a kind and an area, such as `implementation gap (checker)`.
- The earlier text of a changed row is in `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger-history.md`.

Read the ledger only through the queries below: it is too large to read whole.

A row states its gap as it stands now. A note adds a fact. If your work changes what a row says, write the row's whole new line with `rewrite` (below), not a note that tells the repair.

The heading reader of `ledger.py` does not expand the specification's `\Trait{X}` macro. So a row that names a library trait's section cites `Specification-1.0-frozen/` by line.

## Reading the record

Read only the slice of the record that you need. This tool prints whole entries, in parts of bounded size:

    T=explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh

- `$T 'F-87'` prints one entry by its number, and `$T 'P-48'` one of POSITIONS. `$T 'F-87+'` adds each entry that F-87 cites by its number, and each entry that cites F-87. `$T 'history:F-87'` prints its history. Run one when your brief or a note cites an entry by its number.
- `$T 'positions:WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints one of the curator's decisions. Run it before you choose among ways to do something. If several titles hold the words, it names them.
- `$T 'WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints each FACTS entry whose bold title holds them, and `$T 'section:HEADING'` every entry of a FACTS section. Run one before you investigate a behaviour of the tree, and when your brief or a note names an entry. These queries and `positions:` read titles only: before you write that the record does not hold something, also grep FACTS and POSITIONS for its words.
- `$T 'index:WORDS'` prints the INDEX lines that hold the words. Run it to find the notes on a topic.
- `$T 'ledger-find:WORDS'` prints one line for each ledger row that holds every word. Run it when you meet a defect, before you investigate it.
- `$T 'ledger:ROW'` prints one row whole. Run it for each row that you need from a find, your brief or a note.
- `$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'` prints a section of any note, or of a `.tex` chapter, and `$T 'map:FILE#HEADING'` a section of a note under `explorations/coordinator/map/`. Run one when your brief or a note names a section. `#HEADING@WORDS` prints only the table rows and list items of that section that hold every one of WORDS.
- `$T --check QUERY ...` prints only where each query matches and its size. Run it before a query whose size you do not know. `--part N` prints part N of a long output, and `--help` gives the rest.

A word of a query that ends in `*` matches the start of a word. Any other word matches a whole word.

Before you edit a file of the original tree, list the ledger rows that cite it, and read each row that your edit can change:

    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py find --cites FILE

## Writing to the record

- Write FACTS and POSITIONS only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`, never by hand. `add` gives a new entry its number, and `set` rewrites an entry. The tool writes the entry to `FACTS.md` or `POSITIONS.md`, and its earlier text to the history file beside it. It commits nothing: commit both files in one commit. Its header gives its usage.
- If your brief lets you write FACTS, add each fact as a new entry in the section of its topic, in the commit that establishes it. Put its detail in a section of your report: the file:line citations, the commands with their output, and the measured numbers. Point the entry to that section, by your report's file and the section's heading. If your report is only your final message, hand the fact over instead. Spend no effort on the entry's wording: it is rewritten to the record's form after your work.
- If your brief does not let you write FACTS, hand each fact over in the "For FACTS" item of your report, with:
  - the fact as it stands now, in one sentence;
  - what it means for the work;
  - the number that a decision rests on, if any, with what it counts; if its parts belong to different ledger rows, the part of each row;
  - the test that fails if the fact stops holding, or the command and the output that show it;
  - the section of your report that holds the detail.
- If your brief lets you write FACTS, rewrite a wrong entry in place. Otherwise say in your hand-over that the entry is wrong, with the evidence.
- POSITIONS holds each of the curator's decisions, in one place. Everything else points there. Write a decision there only if your brief gives it to you to record. If you have evidence against one, do as `exploring.md` says.
- Put new files of the work under `explorations/`. If you add a note directly in `explorations/` or `explorations/reviews/`, add its line to INDEX: ``- `PATH`: `` and the first sentence of the note's header comment.

Write the gap ledger only with `ledger.py`, which checks each line that it writes against the row template.

    L="python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py"

To add a row:

1. Print the row template, about 3 KB: `$T 'doc:explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md#The row template'`.
2. Write the row as one line in a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with `?` in its number cell.
3. Run `$L add FILE --section TITLE`. It numbers the row and puts it in that section. If the row breaks the template, it adds nothing and prints each rule broken. `$L sections` lists the titles.

To change a row:

- `$L note N TEXT` adds TEXT to the notes of row N. A row at its 1,200-character limit takes no note.
- `$L rewrite N FILE` replaces row N with the whole line in FILE, a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with N or `?` in its number cell. Use it to correct the claim, cut the notes or change the reproducer. The tool checks the line against the template and keeps the old line in the history file.
- `$L duplicate N --of M` makes row N a pointer to row M.
- `$L close N --commit HASH --test NAME` marks row N `FIXED`, by the commit HASH and its test NAME. Run it once that commit is in `HEAD`, and commit the close after it. NAME can also be a file under `explorations/coordinator/tools/`, or `none` with `--note REASON`. For a `CONTESTED` row, add `--settled TEXT`, which names what settled its question.
- `$L landing-check BASE` prints each problem, and exits 1 on any. Run it when your brief asks for it. It checks the whole ledger against the template, so a broken row that BASE already had counts too. The problems are a row that breaks the template, an `XXX` test deleted or renamed while a row that is not closed names it, a row that is not closed though a commit says it fixed it, and a FACTS or POSITIONS entry that disagrees with a row's status.

## The repository's history

- The repository is a 2018 fork of `sirinath/fortress`, a git conversion of the project's java.net Mercurial repository. Its trunk runs from 2007-01-04 to 2012-08-31 and ends at `a874948ac`, the team's last commit.
- The commits after `a874948ac` are the revival's. After the tag `sealed-tree`, commit `75cca6683`, the revival began to fix the team's code, test first. Before it, the revival changed mainly the build and the toolchain.
- `git diff a874948ac -- FILE` shows what the revival changed in a file, and `git diff 75cca6683 -- FILE` what it changed after the tag.
- The conversion cut 146 parent links, so a `git log` of a directory stops at a cut and misses the team's earlier commits. Use `git log --follow` on a file, or compare contents.
- To find who wrote something, or where the repository's history after 2012 comes from, read `research/authorship.md` and `explorations/coordinator/lineage.md`.
- Commit `8fe1daa8f` copied a third-party port of the tree to Java 9 onto the team's last commit, `a874948ac`. Give its lines no credit, and name no author of it in any text that you commit. In a reconstruction of authorship, attribute nothing of it to anyone.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""The record's tool: it owns the form of FACTS.md and POSITIONS.md and of
their two history files, and is the only way to write them.

An entry is one line under a permanent number, `- F-87 **Title.** Text.` in
explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md and `- P-48 **Title.** Text.` in
POSITIONS.md. A number is never reused or changed: a new entry takes the
highest number its file has ever used, plus one. An entry stands under the
nearest `## ` or `### ` heading above it, its section. Its title is its bold
opening, or where it has none, its opening words up to the first colon,
semicolon or full stop.

A pointer is another entry's number in the sentence that needs it, alone
(`It builds P-48.`) or with the first words of the target's title in quotes
(`It builds P-48, "A type parameter the arguments do not fix ..."`, or
`P-48 ("...")`). Quoted words must open the target's current title (`...` or
`…` marks words left out); when an entry is retitled, the tool rewrites them
in every entry that points to it, in the same call.

The history (FACTS-history.md, POSITIONS-history.md beside the record) holds,
under `### F-87`, one block per change, oldest first: one provenance line (the
UTC time from the clock, the kind of change, `from` each report section,
`commit`, `by`, then the note after a colon), and the line as it stood before
the change. The tool derives the kind: `added`, `rewritten`, `moved to "S"`,
`merged into F-n`, `F-n merged in`, `removed`, `noted`; the numbering wrote one
`numbered` block per entry. A retitle that refreshed other entries' pointer
words, or a merge that moved their pointers, says so in one more line of the
block (`pointer words refreshed in: F-12, P-48`).

A `noted` block, which `note` writes, leaves the entry as it is. It adds what
the entry's history lacks, such as the curator's messages behind a text kept
word for word, with their times, or a correction of an earlier block. It holds
no earlier line, and its note says what it adds, so it needs one. A gone entry
takes none: its last block stays `merged into` or `removed`. A noted block
that corrects an earlier block names it by its time, in the field after the
kind: `correcting the block of 2026-10-13 19:07Z`, or, where blocks of the
entry share that minute, `correcting the 2nd block of 2026-10-14 04:41Z`,
counted oldest first. The block corrected is never edited.

Every write takes a lock (flock on .record.lock beside the record), checks the
state it would leave, appends the history blocks first and then replaces each
record file in one step. A write is refused only for what would break the
store: a bad number, a pointer that does not resolve or whose words do not
open its target's title, a line break in an entry, no provenance (neither
`--from` nor `--note`; for a noted block, no `--note`), a correction that
names no block or more than one, two blocks for one entry in one call.
Never for size. The tool does not commit: commit the record file and its
history together.

usage: record.py COMMAND [ARGS] [PROVENANCE] [--root DIR]

  PROVENANCE: --from PATH#HEADING (repeatable; PATH from the repository root
  or from explorations/, HEADING held by exactly one heading of it, as doc:
  resolves one), --commit HASH (in HEAD's history), --by WHO, --note WHY.
  Each write needs --from or --note.

  add F|P --section TITLE FILE   a new entry from FILE's one line, numbered
      record.py add F --section 'Landed semantics' new.md --from 'compile-ladder/rung-x/REPORT.md#The fix' --by coordinator
  set N [FILE] [--section TITLE] entry N rewritten from FILE's line, or moved
      record.py set F-87 f87.md --from 'compile-ladder/rung-x/REPORT.md#The question' --note 'cut to the form'
  merge N --into M [FILE]        N removed, M rewritten from FILE (or kept),
                                 every pointer to N made a pointer to M
      record.py merge F-90 --into F-87 f87.md --note 'one fact, two entries'
  remove N                       N removed; refused while a pointer to it remains
      record.py remove P-131 --note 'evicted to the coordinator skill, references/briefing.md'
  note N [--correcting TIME]     a noted block in N's history, N unchanged; needs
                                 --note; refused when the history holds it already.
                                 TIME: 2026-10-13 19:07Z, or 2nd 2026-10-14 04:41Z
      record.py note P-25 --from 'positions-audit/full/evidence/corrections-c1.md#History lines the tool cannot write' --note 'his message behind the text: 2026-09-26T08:01:03.475Z, ...'
      record.py note P-7 --correcting '2026-10-13 19:07Z' --commit b87a17de5 --note 'that block names bc8902f47, ...'
  apply FILE                     many changes from one file, all or none (below)
      record.py apply chunk3.md --by 'consolidation chunk 3'
  check [--base COMMIT]          the store's checks; exit 1 on a failure
      record.py check --base cc9424c2a

An apply file holds, in any order: `## TITLE` or `### TITLE`, the section the
new entries below it go to (an existing entry stands under no heading, or
under its own section's, or the `## ` one that holds it); entry lines as they
should stand, `- F-87 ...`, or `- F-?1 ...` for a new entry, its placeholder
replaced by its number everywhere in the file; `move F-87 to SECTION`;
`remove F-90`; `merge F-91 into F-87`; `note F-87`, or `note F-87 correcting
TIME`, a noted block. Each may be followed by one indented provenance line of
its own:
`  from: PATH, "HEADING"; commit: HASH; by: WHO; note: WHY`. Blank lines and
`<!-- -->` comments are ignored. An entry line equal to the entry is skipped:
to add to its history, write `note F-87`. A note whose block the history holds
already, all but its time, is skipped too, so a file run twice writes nothing
twice. One call writes one block per entry, so an entry is noted, or changed,
once in a file.

check fails on: an entry line without its number, or a line under an entry
that continues it; a number on two lines; a number with no `numbered` or
`added` block, or one gone from its file whose last block is not `merged into`
or `removed`; a noted block that holds an earlier line, or whose `correcting`
names no earlier block of its entry, or more than one; a pointer to no live
entry, or quoted words that do not open the target's title; with --base, an
entry at COMMIT that is neither its line now nor the earlier line of a block
in its history (pointer words refreshed by the tool aside). It reports, without failing: the entries over 600 characters, the
entries without a bold title, and the `--from` paths and the report sections
an entry cites (`PATH`, "HEADING") that do not resolve.

The reads are facts-extract.sh's: `F-87`, `F-87+` (with the entries it points
to and that point to it), `history:F-87`, and the title queries, which fall
back to the former titles in the history.
"""

12:- P-12 **After the switch-over, walk runs the compiled type checker on its programs, and then uses the static coercions that the checker inserts.** The curator wants the checker usable on the programs that walk runs. Today `fortress typecheck` checks a program only against the compiler's prelude, so it is no check of walk's programs (F-9 holds this fact). Walk is not changed for this before the switch-over. After it, walk runs the checker on its programs and so gains their static types. Walk then uses the static coercions that the checker inserts, in place of its choice on the run-time value (P-59, walk's choice of coercions until the switch-over).

16:- P-17 **Unboxed doubles and arrays of unboxed doubles are required: without them the revival misses its point.** Why: a language meant for high performance cannot box its numbers. Today the code generator boxes every number: an `RR64` value is an object of the class `FRR64`. In Java models of microGPT's three array kernels, the dot product, the matrix product and the row lift, boxing is the main cost (F-11 holds the measurement). How arrays store doubles, as `double[]`, is P-84's decision.

23:- P-25 **`Specification/` stays the standard, and the Types chapter of the team's 2012 restart is cited beside it.** The restart is a new specification that the team began in 2012 and left unfinished (F-166). Where its Types chapter, `Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick`, covers a topic, a worker cites it beside `Specification/` as the designers' later word. On the rules that the revival revises, such as the exclusion rule, the chapter is the designers' latest intent, which the goal is to finish, and `Specification/` is revised to follow it (P-26: the specification is revised to the team's later word). Three of the chapter's passages bear on that revision (P-97 holds how the revision uses them). It names the exclusion rule "instantiation exclusion" and gives it in two parts: which instantiations of a generic exclude each other (`types.tick:355-360`), and, in its note, a rule on trait declarations (`:361-376`). The revised `Specification/` takes that form: the first part in its chapter on types, the second in its chapter on traits. It adds a `covariant` modifier for a trait's static parameters, which neither path implements and which is future work, off the path to microGPT (P-62). It says that `Bottom` cannot be written in a program.

28:- P-30 **The check of microGPT under walk after a batch must take less than a minute.** That is the curator's goal. The check runs about two forward-and-backward passes of the model and compares the results with reference values. That is enough to show that the model's mathematics still works, and that the library's changes, such as those to the arrays, did not break it. A slower check is to him a waste of time. Each batch's commit stage runs the check as `explorations/coordinator/tools/mg-run.sh`, the quick versions of microGPT's two programs at once, outside the gate.

29:- P-32 **The record's maps are kept current and used, so that nothing that the record holds is worked out again from scratch.** The maps are `FACTS.md`, `INDEX.md` and the territory map, `explorations/coordinator/map/`. The territory map surveys the repository down to where the team wrote the intent of each design. Part of that intent is written only in the papers under `Papers/`, not in the specification. So the map covers the papers too, and shows where to look up a design's intent. How the maps are read is the `coordinator` skill's: FACTS and `INDEX.md` whole at the coordinator's boot ("The boot"), and the territory map as each rung's mission briefing (`references/batch.md`). The territory map's surveys date from 2026-09-16 (its README), so a status or a line number in them can be stale.

30:- P-33 **The work toward microGPT compiled follows the phases, in the order that the curator approved.** Phase 3, the compiled checker reports no error on the interpreter's whole library (the distance to the switch-over at zero; F-53 defines it and holds its value); phase 4, the switch-over, first the natives, the library's `builtinPrimitive` bindings made to run on the compiled path, then the compiled path reads the interpreter's library and the compiler's prelude is deleted; phase 5, microGPT compiles: its static types, the array design and the code generator's open gaps; phase 6, microGPT runs fast. Other work has gone in beside that order. The repair batch from the reviews of the landed batches went in before phase 3: on 2026-09-27 he said that those reviews could yield batches that go in before phase 3. Code-generator work goes on under either library (P-37). One decision that an agent took without his approval: row 320 has two halves. The agent fixed one, mutability across the api, and gated the other as an expected failure instead of fixing it (`ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/XXXExportVarRungXLinked`): an api implemented by a component of another name does not link.

36:- P-39 **Every batch's gate measures the checker count, and its total never turns the gate red.** The checker count and the distance to the switch-over both count the compiled checker's errors on the interpreter's library. The count stops where the checker crashes or meets an error that it cannot get past; the distance counts every error, over all apis and components (F-53 defines both and holds their values). A rise of the count's total is reported and never fails a batch on its own. The count's stage, step 8 of the batch's gate (`explorations/coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.md`), can still turn the gate red on the faults that F-66 names. One is a checker crash that no rung of the batch listed in advance as expected, in the field `expectedCheckerCrash` of its manifest. The gates of batches whose work drives the distance down also measure the distance, in a stage that only reports. Why: the distance's full measurement takes far longer than the count, and a batch pays for it only when the distance is the number that it tries to move.

37:- P-40 **Sizes are checked, and a size that inference leaves unknown is an error only where it is used.** A size is a `nat` or `int` static parameter, such as the length of an array in its type. The compiled checker checks sizes, and refuses a size beyond `NN32` or `ZZ32` (F-140, the bound on both paths). Wherever the array design creates a JVM array, it checks the length there, at run time, and refuses one over 2^31-1. A size that inference leaves unknown is an error only when it reaches a type, a name or a value. So a declaration may declare a size that none of its types uses, and pass. A call that cannot fix a size of the declaration that it would choose is refused, also inside an overload set, instead of passing over that declaration. In the rule that no type extends two different instantiations of one generic trait, two instantiations differ when any static argument but an operator differs, so `Vec[\3\]` and `Vec[\4\]` are two; boolean arguments count too once the checker has boolean parameters. A size used as a number, as in the range `0#n`, converts to `ZZ32` where one is needed, as a numeral does. The 17 vector and matrix operators of the `FortressLibrary` api lose their unused sizes by `explorations/perf-probes/array-sites/e3-rebased.patch`, which finishes the team's own fix of 2008: that fix removed them from the component only. The JVM length check waits for the array design; under walk such an array dies with a raw Java exception (row 527). The checker still passes over a declaration whose unfixed size occurs in its own parameter type (row 400). The checker compares no boolean arguments (row 406).

42:- P-45 **Overloaded declarations may differ in their static parameters.** The specification drops its sentence that forbids this, and keeps it as superseded text. It states instead the overloading model of the type group's 2011 paper (`Papers/Types/`), which the compiled checker already used. The checker keeps the paper's three rules: No Duplicates, Meet and Return Type. It checks the Return Type Rule over every instance of a generic declaration that the argument types allow, not over one guessed instance. One rule of the old sentence survives: if one generic declaration is more specific than another, their static parameters must line up position by position, as Java's rule for overriding a generic method requires. Walk chooses among overloads by the parameter types that each declaration declares, not by the order in which they are written. At load, walk judges each pair of two generic declarations by the checker's rules on their declared parameter types. It does not refuse a pair only because none of their parameter types exclude, as when one declaration is more specific than the other. Walk and the checker must accept the same pairs. The library repairs, by declarations of its own, the overload sets that the checker refused, and no line of microGPT's two programs changes. Where walk or the checker still judges a pair against these rules: walk compares two functional methods of a generic trait or object on the instance that a call makes (F-26); both paths refuse the paper's own valid example (row 539); walk refuses two nested generic functional methods of a plain trait, and fails at a call on them in a generic trait (rows 779 and 780); and walk and the checker disagree on four kinds of pair (rows 759 and 786 to 788).

43:- P-46 **A conversion only makes a call possible: it never changes which declaration runs when one already fits.** The declaration that runs is chosen on the parameter types that each overload declares: first those that apply, then the most specific of them (P-45). A generic declaration applies if some type within its bounds takes the arguments. Only then is the chosen declaration instantiated by promotion: at the narrowest type into which its arguments coerce (P-74). So beside `op(a: Any, b: Any)`, `op[\T extends Number\](a: T, b: T)` applies to a call with a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64`, at `T = Number`. It is the more specific, so it runs, at `ZZ64`. Why: the curator wants fast generic code that a JVM can specialise. His own broader rule is not taken: to apply any conversion that reaches a specific declaration, and to fall back to a plain one only when none does. Walk and the compiled checker both infer static arguments with coercion, by the same promotion. The compiled path inserts the conversions statically. Walk, which has no static types, promotes from the arguments' run-time types: a choice taken without the curator's word. P-49 gives the order in which the checker tries a call. Row 537: the compiled dispatch between two generic declarations of one name with different bounds.

45:- P-48 **A type parameter that a call's arguments do not fix takes its bound, never `Bottom`.** The arguments leave a parameter unfixed when it occurs only in the result type; when two arguments meet at it with no narrowest type into which both convert (a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64` have one, `ZZ64`, by P-74); or when dispatch, at run time, picks a generic declaration and must choose the instance to run. Its instance is then the intersection of its upper bounds (`Any` if it has none). At checking, that is narrowed by what the call's expected type (P-49 defines it) requires of the declared return type; at run time, by the static type that the checker gave the call. It is never `Bottom`, never the union of the arguments' types, and never the value's type alone. The rule sets the instance, not which declaration runs (P-46). Why: the rule is the team's later word, from the POPL 2019 paper on multiple dispatch, and the curator trusts the team's later work above his own understanding (P-26). The rule changes nothing in microGPT, whose types are concrete. The library keeps the team's declarations of `fail`, `builtinPrimitive` and `List`'s empty comprehension, whose type parameters have no written bound, without the `extends Object` that a batch had added. Under walk, dispatch takes the value's type, and always will, since walk has no static types. Row 538: a compiled dispatcher that carries the static type that the checker gave the call, so that a generic declaration reached only at run time gets this instance. Rows 587, 591 and 612: three cases in which walk still gives `Bottom` (walk's `Bottom` for row 591 kept without the curator's word).

46:- P-49 **The compiled checker tries a call first by subtyping, without the expected type, and coerces its arguments only when that attempt is not kept.** The expected type is the type that the call's context requires. The checker's first attempt checks the call by subtyping alone, without the expected type. It keeps that attempt when its result converts to the expected type, by coercion if need be. If it does not keep that attempt, it tries coercion of the arguments, with the expected type. So a declaration that fits the arguments as they are is not passed over for one that coercion reaches. Why: in the curator's words, coercion should be tried when there are no matches. Between the two, the checker tries subtyping with the expected type, a choice taken without the curator's word. Last, it tries coercion without the expected type (`compile-ladder/rung-instance-bound/decision-record.md`, D4, the built order).

51:- P-54 **`QQ`'s `ceiling` and `truncate` keep `ZZ`, their declared result type, and raise an error at +∞, −∞ and 0/0.** The specification's paragraph on these methods said that they return the argument itself at those three values (`Specification/basic-lib/numbers.tex`, "Rational Numbers"). That paragraph is revised. `floor`, `round` and the brackets ⌊x⌋ and ⌈x⌉ are built on `ceiling` and `truncate`, so they raise too. Why: the declared integer result and other languages win over the paragraph: Python's `math.floor(inf)`, for one, raises. The library raises `DivisionByZero`, as the revised paragraph says. Later, a rung after the switch-over makes `QQ` follow the float ruling (P-68, on rounding the float types). Then `floor` and `ceiling` return `QQ` and pass the infinities through, and the brackets, `round` and `truncate` give `ZZ`.

55:- P-58 **Every native binding is a `builtinPrimitive` call naming a static helper.** A native binding is a library body that is exactly `builtinPrimitive("…")`, the library's own form, and it keeps that form. Its string is to name a static Java method in `nativeHelpers/`, the compiled path's helpers, such as `"com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleIntArith.intLT"`, in place of a glue class of walk, which the compiled path cannot use (F-32). Walk is to load the named helper through a loader beside its glue classes. At the parse, before the checker, the compiled path is to rewrite each such body into a synthetic `import java` of the helper and a call, and to refuse a string that names no helper. The bindings move onto helpers rung by rung, and the compiled checker sees each rung's bindings as that rung lands, not all at once at the switch-over. The other form, `import java` declarations written in the library itself, is not taken. Every binding still names a glue class, and neither the loader nor the rewrite exists. The first natives rung builds them, test first, and the later rungs move the bindings.

57:- P-60 **The specification reads a `comprises` clause at the level of values.** `trait S comprises { U, V }` says that every value of `S` is a value of `U` or of `V`. So another trait may stand between `S` and its listed types. The specification defines "covers" once: a type covers another when every value of the second is a value of the first. The Meet Rule gains a case for closed traits. Where the rule asks for a declaration at the meet of two overloads' parameter types, several declarations below both serve, if together they cover the meet. So a call whose argument's static type stands between closed traits and their listed types may have several most specific declarations. The call's type is the intersection of their return types, and the declaration that runs is unique only at run time. Why: the proof addendum (`reviews/comprises-type-level-proof-addendum.md`) shows this sound for ground declarations, at calls that need no coercion. A ground declaration's types hold no type variable, and `G[\ZZ32\]` is ground. The addendum also asks that the checker use coverage only in its overloading rules, to accept an overload set and to justify a call's tie among several most specific declarations, and not in its general subtype test. A declaration with static parameters, whose instance dispatch must choose at run time, is outside the proof: one instance would have to meet every one of the return types at once. The typing by the intersection is not extended to it, and the specification states that boundary.

77:- P-73 **Under walk, fixed-width integer arithmetic raises `IntegerOverflow` when its result does not fit, on the unsigned `NN32` and `NN64` too.** The rule covers every operation whose result can leave its type, `^`, `CHOOSE` and `LCM` included (F-132 holds what is built and its tests). So a subtraction below 0 on `NN32` raises. Code that means to wrap uses the specification's wrapping operators ∔ (`DOTPLUS`), ∸ (`DOTMINUS`) and ⨰ (`DOTTIMES`), fully parenthesised, since the specification states their precedence only among the three. The specification's saturating operators, such as ⊞ (`BOXPLUS`), are not in the interpreter's library; they wait for a later step of their own. Why: this is the specification's rule, and the compiled path already raised the error for addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, negation and absolute value on `ZZ32` and `ZZ64`.

79:- P-75 **`NN32` coerces into `RR64` implicitly, since every `NN32` value converts to `RR64` exactly.** Why: a conversion that fits is implicit, the rule of P-74 on mixed widths. With the coercion, an operator that both `RR64` and `ZZ64` declare is ambiguous on both paths for a `ZZ32` with an `NN32`, since neither `ZZ64` nor `RR64` coerces into the other. Without it, P-74's rule, the narrowest type into which both arguments coerce, gives `ZZ64` (row 575 holds the conflict and its measurement). Each way to build it changes a decided behaviour.

82:- P-78 **`SUM` and `PROD` are one generic reduction each over the library's algebra, in place of the team's catch-all over `Number`, and take their identity from the static argument.** `SUM` is generic over `AdditiveGroup` and `PROD` over `MultiplicativeRing`. A reduction written with generators writes its static argument where its generators and body do not fix the element type, as in `SUM[\ZZ32\][j <- 0#n] f(j)`. A declared type that receives the value does not fix it: the compiled checker refuses the call without the static argument even then (row 731). A sum without generators is written as before, with no static argument: `SUM e` over a collection `e`, and the dot product `x DOT y`. `BIG MAXN`, `BIG MINN` and `BIG MINMAXN`, the team's `Number`-typed big operators for the maximum, the minimum and both, each with an identity, are gone; no program called them. `MAX` and `MIN` get no identity on the integers or the floats, so an empty `BIG MAX` or `BIG MIN` raises `EmptyReduction` (F-60: a maximum's identity is its type's least value, which a coercion into a wider type does not carry). Under walk, an empty `SUM` or `PROD` over another algebra, such as a user `AdditiveGroup`, still fails (row 436) until the specification's `HasIdentity` is built.

83:- P-79 **Every team demo is kept running as the tree changes.** The team demos are the programs in `ProjectFortress/demos/`. If a change breaks a demo and the way to repair the demo is known, the same batch rewrites the demo. For example, the change that made `10^(-4)` an error (P-153, the integer power) also wrote `10.0^(-4)` in `BiCGSTAB.fss` and `BiCGSTAB2.fss`, and `10.0^(-6)` for `10^(-6)` in `npbft.fss`. A demo that fails for want of a feature is made to run again once the feature is built. So the demos known to fail today are to be respelled where the way is known: the five demos that walk refuses at load, since they leave an inherited abstract method without a body (row 670, which names them); `trips.fss`, which walk runs but the compiled checker refuses, since its `generator` object extends `StandardTotalOrder[\trip\]` without being a `trip` (row 710); the timing line of `BiCGSTAB.fss` and `BiCGSTAB2.fss`, which divides a `ZZ64` by a float and so stops walk (row 791); and the reductions that the compiled checker refuses because they leave out the static argument of a big operator whose bound names its own static parameter, such as `SUM`; their repair writes the argument (row 731).

89:- P-84 **An `RR64` array is stored as a Java `double[]`, unboxed, and arrays keep the team's `nat` sizes in their types.** Why: a high-performance language cannot box its array elements, and the sizes are central to the team's design. So the storage and the sizes are one design: the sizes stay in the array types as `nat` static parameters, as the library's `Vector` and `Matrix` declare them, and the compiled checker checks them. The sizes do not wait while a first version of the store carries them only as run-time fields; that layered plan was rejected. Both halves follow the library's own patterns (P-27, the library's own practice is the standard). The compiled checker checks `nat` static parameters (F-67). The compiled path's `double[]` store waits with the other array decisions until after the switch-over; among them is decision A, the way the `double[]` store goes under a float vector (P-85).

90:- P-85 **The array design's three questions are open, with no default, and return after the switch-over with the array decisions A, B and D.** The array design is the compiled path's design for arrays. The three questions: whether the array factory chooses a store for each element type; whether the store also keeps the size as a field, beside the size in the type; and whether a factory for a size known only at run time returns the unsized `Array[\E,I\]`, whose type holds no size. These questions are apart from decisions A, B and D: decision A is how the `double[]` store goes under a float vector, B is where unboxed arithmetic happens, and D is the sizes in the model's own types (P-87). The whole preparation for the array work is to be done before the switch-over; only the work itself waits. One exception to "no default": on the third question's ground, an agent has since landed a default in the tree, way 4a, by which the compiled checker reads a size known only at run time as fixed for that call, not as unknown. It is not the curator's answer.

92:- P-88 **The model's vocabulary leaves `+`, `-` and `MAX` between an array and a scalar to the library's scalar-extension block, and its diagonal keeps its own product.** The vocabulary, the array operations that microGPT is written in, declares none of these six operators, an array with a number on either side; the library's scalar-extension block, in `Library/FortressLibrary.fss`, serves them. `Diag`, the vocabulary's diagonal matrix, extends `Matrix` and overrides `mul`, the method that the library's matrix product calls, so `diag(v) m` scales the rows of `m` without forming the matrix. This is what the type system promises: a diagonal is a kind of matrix, with a faster product of its own. Row 299 records what the general product costs on a diagonal: 13 to 54 times as much as scaling the rows. Since the diagonal is read-only, a read-only matrix trait, `ReadableArray2`, which `Array2` would extend as `Array1` extends `ReadableArray1`, is also wanted: it is a library change, not a definition in the vocabulary.

100:- P-96 **A change of the specification is shown in layers, as the team showed its own changes in the 1.0 release of 2008 and in the working draft of 2009.** This form is the revision form; P-80 and P-147 call it the S1 form. A callout that prints in every build marks each changed passage; a `\note` will not do, since a release build hides it. Appendix I's revival section has an entry for each change: its reason, its original text, what a return to route C would mean for it (P-95 says what route C is), and the decision that it follows. The front matter has one paragraph on the revision, and a document in the repository holds the full reasoning. Citations call the unrevised copy, `Specification-1.0-frozen/`, the Working Draft of February 2011: the copy is that draft byte for byte, and only its `fortress.1.0.pdf` is the 1.0 release (F-163). The `fortress-repo` skill's `references/specification.md` gives each part in full, including what else an Appendix I entry holds.

63:- P-151 **Only the `where`-clause forms that the team wrote down are built: conditional extension, a function's or a method's condition, and `AnyList`'s `comprises` clause.** A `where` clause states conditions on static parameters, and may introduce static variables of its own, as `where [\E\]` does. A trait or object that extends a type under a `where` condition is that type only where the condition holds, and its members are checked with the condition holding (conditional extension). A `where` condition on a function's or a method's own static parameters bounds them. ## The row template

A row is one line of eight cells, `| # | claim | status | class | spec citation | reproducer | found by | notes / workaround |`, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of its topic section, in number order. A pipe inside a cell is written `\|`. (POSITIONS, "The gap ledger's form"; the proposal behind it is `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/gap-ledger-archaeology.md`, section 4.)

- **#**: the row's number, the next free one when it is added; never reused, renumbered or given to another row. 148 is vacant.
- **claim**: at most 300 characters, whose first 150 name the defect or the capability: what fails or what holds, and where.
- **status**: exactly one word of seven, with no second status and nothing in brackets:
  - `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`: it works; it ran and its output is recorded.
  - `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`: the specification settles it and the reproducer confirms it. A row with one half fixed stays `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, and its notes say which half is fixed.
  - `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`: the failure reproduces; the mechanisms tried are named and are not exhaustive.
  - `CONTESTED`: unsettled; the notes say why.
  - `RETIRED`: a source's claim falsified here, kept so that it is not derived again.
  - `FIXED`: closed by a landed commit (`ledger.py close`): the claim's first sentence, the test as reproducer, notes `fixed HASH; full text: history, row N`.
  - `DUPLICATE`: a pointer (`ledger.py duplicate`), notes `duplicate of row M; full text: history, row N`.
- **class**: `kind (area)`; `—` only for `POSITIVE-VERIFIED` and `RETIRED`. The kind is one of `implementation gap`, `library gap vs spec`, `library bug`, `design limit`, `deliberate`, `typesetter`, `packaging`; the area one of `parser`, `walk`, `checker`, `codegen`, `runtime`, `library`, `prelude`, `specification`, `tests`, `tools`.
- **spec citation**: the `.tex` file and the section heading in quotes, as `basic/operators/juxtameaning.tex`, "Juxtaposition"; a line number only against `Specification-1.0-frozen/`; `silent` where the specification does not say.
- **reproducer**: one test (its name, or its path under the test folders; an `XXX` test while it is an expected failure) or one probe path from the repository root, at most 200 characters; `none` when nothing in the tree reproduces it, with the command and its output, or the probe's old path, in the notes.
- **found by**: the stream that found it (`climb batch 8 rung I`, `run-c3`, `apl rung 2`), at most 60 characters; no date and no role.
- **notes / workaround**: at most 700 characters: `siblings: N, M` first if there are any; the mechanism, with file:line and the commit it was true at; the workaround; for a closed row, `fixed HASH`.

A path under `explorations/` that is no longer in the tree is read from history: `git show $(git log -1 --diff-filter=D --format=%h -- PATH)^:PATH`.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""The gap ledger's tool: it owns the ledger's format, reads its rows, and is
the only way to write them.

The ledger, explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md, is sorted into topic sections,
each a "## TITLE" heading over one table of rows. A row is one line of eight
cells, and keeps its number wherever it sits:

  | # | claim | status | class | spec citation | reproducer | found by | notes / workaround |

The template (POSITIONS.md, "The gap ledger's form"; the proposal behind it is
explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/gap-ledger-archaeology.md, 4.1):
  status       exactly one of POSITIVE-VERIFIED, NEGATIVE-VERIFIED,
               NEGATIVE-BOUNDED, CONTESTED, RETIRED, FIXED, DUPLICATE
  class        `kind (area)`, kind one of the legend's seven, area one of ten;
               `—` only for POSITIVE-VERIFIED and RETIRED
  spec         the .tex file and the section heading in quotes; a line number
               only against Specification-1.0-frozen/; `silent` where the
               specification does not say
  reproducer   one test (a name under the test folders, or a path) or probe
               path from the repository root, or `none`
  limits       row 1,200 characters, claim 300, reproducer 200, found by 60,
               notes 700
  a pipe inside a cell is written \\|

Cells are split only at a pipe that is not escaped as \\|. A row whose cells
hold bare pipes (the ledger had six) does not split into its table's width that
way; it is read by its split at pipes followed by a space or the line's end, as
facts-extract.py has always read it, and check reports it under `pipe`.

Every write takes a lock (flock on .ledger.lock beside the ledger), checks the
template on the line it writes, and puts the full earlier line of a row it
changes, unchanged, in the history file beside the ledger
(fortress-gap-ledger-history.md), under "### Row N" and a line saying what
became of it. A failed check prints the rules the row breaks and exits 1.
add, rewrite, close and duplicate check the whole line they write; note checks
only what it changes (the notes cell and the row's length), so that a row
failing the template elsewhere still takes a note. A row at its length limit
takes no note: rewrite cuts it back (the rework's decision D4, "each is cut
when next edited", process-engineering/gap-ledger-archaeology.md).

POSITIONS.md:43
- P-46 **A conversion only makes a call possible: it never changes which declaration runs when one already fits.** The declaration that runs is chosen on the parameter types that each overload declares: first those that apply, then the most specific of them (P-45). A generic declaration applies if some type within its bounds takes the arguments. Only then is the chosen declaration instantiated by promotion: at the narrowest type into which its arguments coerce (P-74). So beside `op(a: Any, b: Any)`, `op[\T extends Number\](a: T, b: T)` applies to a call with a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64`, at `T = Number`. It is the more specific, so it runs, at `ZZ64`. Why: the curator wants fast generic code that a JVM can specialise. His own broader rule is not taken: to apply any conversion that reaches a specific declaration, and to fall back to a plain one only when none does. Walk and the compiled checker both infer static arguments with coercion, by the same promotion. The compiled path inserts the conversions statically. Walk, which has no static types, promotes from the arguments' run-time types: a choice taken without the curator's word. P-49 gives the order in which the checker tries a call. == explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### The one library and the compiled checker; P-46 points to it

POSITIONS.md:42
- P-45 **Overloaded declarations may differ in their static parameters.** The specification drops its sentence that forbids this, and keeps it as superseded text. It states instead the overloading model of the type group's 2011 paper (`Papers/Types/`), which the compiled checker already used. The checker keeps the paper's three rules: No Duplicates, Meet and Return Type. It checks the Return Type Rule over every instance of a generic declaration that the argument types allow, not over one guessed instance. One rule of the old sentence survives: if one generic declaration is more specific than another, their static parameters must line up position by position, as Java's rule for overriding a generic method requires. Walk chooses among overloads by the parameter types that each declaration declares, not by the order in which they are written. At load, walk judges each pair of two generic declarations by the checker's rules on their declared parameter types. It does not refuse a pair only because none of their parameter types exclude, as when one declaration is more specific than the other. Walk and the checker must accept the same pairs. The library repairs, by declarations of its own, the overload sets that the checker refused, and no line of microGPT's two programs changes. Where walk or the checker still judges a pair against these rules: walk compares two functional methods of a generic trait or object on the instance that a call makes (F-26); both paths refuse the paper's own valid example (row 539); walk refuses two nested generic functional methods of a plain trait, and fails at a call on them in a generic trait (rows 779 and 780); and walk and the checker disagree on four kinds of pair (rows 759 and 786 to 788).

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### The one library and the compiled checker

POSITIONS.md:56
- P-59 **Walk chooses a coercion by the run-time value until it runs the checker, after the switch-over.** Walk has no static types. So where a coercion is needed, walk chooses it by the value's run-time type. The specification and the compiled path choose it by the static type. The curator accepts this as the interpreter's limit, and walk is not changed for it before the switch-over. A callout in the coercion chapter (`Specification/basic/conversions-coercions.tex`) states the limit. Two expected-failure tests record it: `XXXCoercionStaticRungC`, the chapter's own printed example, and `XXXCoercionStaticNarrowRungC`. After the switch-over, once walk runs the checker on its programs (P-12 orders the two steps), it uses the static coercions that the checker inserts. MicroGPT's static types are concrete, each the type of the value itself and not a trait above it, so on microGPT walk's choice and the static choice agree.

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### Numbers

POSITIONS.md:72
- P-68 **On the float types, `floor` and `ceiling` return the same float type, while the brackets ⌊x⌋ and ⌈x⌉, `round` and `truncate` return `ZZ`, the unbounded integer.** So `floor(2.5)` is the `RR64` value 2.0, and ⌊2.5⌋ is to be the `ZZ` value 2. Row 330: one library rung after the switch-over, which first counts the interpreter tests whose output changes, then makes the brackets, `round` and `truncate` return `ZZ` in each of the library's declarations of them; today the brackets are `ZZ64` under walk and `RR64` compiled, and `round` and `truncate` are `ZZ64`, `ZZ` or `RR64` by declaration.

== explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md, ## Execution model

FACTS.md:8
- F-9 **`fortress typecheck` checks a program against the compiler's library, `Library/CompilerLibrary.fsi`, so it is no oracle for walk programs.** `Shell.java` calls `useCompilerLibraries()` for the command (row 69). The checker reaches walk's programs after the switch-over (P-12).

# Setting up, building, the caches, and what to rebuild

**tree**
: Checkout of the repository: the main checkout or a worktree. In a command, `<tree>` is the tree that you work in: the one that your brief names, else the one that your session starts in.

**library order**
: Five compiles that build the compiled path's library into the caches.

**DSL grammar**
: `grammar` declaration in an api, which adds syntax for a domain-specific language.

**parser directory**
: New `fortress<random>rats` folder of 5.8 MB, in which a program that imports a DSL grammar gets a Rats! parser generated when it runs. The run makes it in its JVM's temporary directory and never deletes it.

## Setting up each call

Start every Bash call with these lines. They put you at the tree's root, where this skill's commands start unless they `cd`:

    cd <tree> && mkdir -p tmp
    export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64 PATH=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64/bin:$PATH
    export FORTRESS_HOME=$PWD FORTRESS_THREADS=1 TMPDIR=$PWD/tmp JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx4g -Xss64m -Djava.io.tmpdir=$PWD/tmp"
    unset JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS

- If `/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64` or `ant` is missing, run `apt-get update -qq && apt-get install -y openjdk-25-jdk-headless ant` first.
- `bin/fortress` takes `FORTRESS_HOME` from the shell whenever it is set. If it names another tree, you run that tree's code. Check it with `echo $FORTRESS_HOME`.
- `JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS` is unset, because the proxy's trust-store flags in it break ant's JVM forks.

The lines give the settings of `explorations/experiment/env.sh`, with two differences:

- The JVM's temporary directory is your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
- They leave out env.sh's removal of old parser directories in `/tmp`, because your runs put theirs in your tree's `tmp/` (below).

If your brief tells you to run `source env.sh` and then to point `TMPDIR` and `JAVA_FLAGS` at `tmp/`, use the lines above. They do the same.

The library and microGPT import no DSL grammar, and of the gated tests only `ProjectFortress/syntax_abstraction_tests/ForUse.fss` does. The ungated tests beside it import one, and so do the APL experiments under `explorations/apl/`.

With the lines above, your runs that import a DSL grammar put their parser directories in `<tree>/tmp/`. Hundreds of them once filled the disk allowance. So:

- When no run of yours is live, remove yours: `rm -rf <tree>/tmp/fortress*rats`.
- Before a long run, check `df -h /`. How to read it: the `cloud-container` skill.

## Two layers of code

The repository holds two layers of code. Different tools build them, at different times, so "compile" means a different thing in each layer.

The implementation is the parser, walk, the compiled checker, the code generator and the run time. It is the Java and Scala under `ProjectFortress/src/`, with the parser grammars (`parser/*.rats`) and the syntax tree generated from `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast`. `ant compileAll` builds it into `ProjectFortress/build/` ("Building", below). `ant compile` is another name for it.

The Fortress code is the library, the tests and the programs: the `.fss` and `.fsi` files. The `fortress` commands run the phases on it and keep the results in the caches:

- Walk runs the phases on each component that a run needs. It needs no `fortress compile`.
- `fortress compile` writes a component's jar. It is for the compiled path's components only: the compiler's library, compiled tests and compiled programs.
- `fortress run` compiles no Fortress source.
- A command reuses an entry if no source that the entry depends on is newer than the entry: its own source, and the `.fsi` files of the apis that it imports, at any depth.

An edit makes stale what was built from it:

- Java or Scala: the classes in `ProjectFortress/build/`. Run `ant compileAll`. The cache entries that the edited code wrote are stale too, and no entry notices it: an entry is compared with its sources, never with the implementation. For example, after a change to a native helper's signature, its old wrapper stays in `nativewrapper_cache/`, and the run links the old signature. For this reason, the build deletes the caches when the implementation changes ("Building").
- A parser grammar: the generated parser, and every entry that it parsed. Run `ant compileAll`.
- A `.fss` or `.fsi` file of the library: the entries of that component, and after an `.fsi` edit, the entries of every component that imports the api. Walk analyses them again by itself. A component of the compiler's library needs a compile, or the library order ("After an edit of the library").
- A test or a program: its own entries. Walk and the harness analyse a walk test again by themselves. Compile a compiled test or program again, or let the harness do it.

arrow types,

\item
function types, and

\item
three special types:
\TYP{Any}, \TYP{BottomType} and \TYP{()}.

\end{itemize}

Object expression types, function types and \TYP{BottomType}
are not first-class types: they cannot be written in a program.
However, some values have object expression types and function types
and \KWD{throw} and \KWD{exit} expressions have the type \TYP{BottomType}.

Collectively,
trait types and object expression types are \emph{defined} types;
% the trait and object declarations and object expressions
% are the types' \emph{definitions}.

\newsec{\Any, \Bottom\ and the Type Hierarchy}{type-hierarchy}
\seclabel{bottom-type}

Types are partially ordered by subtyping (see \secref{subtyping}),
which defines the \emph{type hierarchy}.
\Any\ is the top of the type hierarchy:
every type is a subtype of \Any\
and every value belongs to \Any.
% and every value is an instance of \Any.
The only type that \Any\ excludes is \Bottom.

\Bottom\ is the bottom of the type hierarchy:
every type is a supertype of \Bottom.
It is \emph{uninhabited}: 
% Do we want to define this term?  
% I don't know that we use it anywhere.
no value belongs to \Bottom,  
%no value is an instance of \Bottom
and \Bottom\ excludes every type (including itself).
\Bottom\ is the only type that excludes itself.
\Bottom\ is also inexpressible:
it cannot be written in a program 
(see \secref{expressible-types})

93:- Do not take or record a timing of walk. Do not edit anything to make walk faster.
98:MicroGPT runs only under walk, by hand, never in the gate. Check the model when your brief asks for it: run your tree's `explorations/coordinator/tools/mg-run.sh <work-dir> <label> [threads]`. `<work-dir>` is a folder under your tree's `tmp/`, and `threads` sets `FORTRESS_THREADS`, 1 by default. The script runs the quick pair at once, `MicroGptFlatQuick.fss` and `MicroGptAplQuick.fss`: two forward and backward passes each, against the reference values, in about 56 s for both. Each starts from
100:- Add the word `full` only if your brief asks for it. It runs the full pair, `MicroGptFlatCheck.fss` and `MicroGptAplCheck.fss`, with 40 checks each and a 90-minute timeout.
#!/bin/bash
# mg-run.sh <work-dir> <label> [threads] [full]: the two microGPT checks under walk, each from an empty
# private cache (FORTRESS_CACHES) in a fresh folder under <work-dir> (old runs' folders stay; clear them by hand), each run from its own directory as its header says, both at once,
# with bin/fortress's own JVM (JAVA_FLAGS -Xmx4g -Xss64m) and FORTRESS_THREADS=<threads> (default 1).
# By default the quick pair, MicroGptFlatQuick and MicroGptAplQuick: two forward-and-backward passes each, 7 checks against the goldens,
# timeout 600 s.  With the word full in any position, the full pair, MicroGptFlatCheck and MicroGptAplCheck: 40 checks each, timeout 5400 s.
# Output to <work-dir>/<name>.txt, headed by the machine line (machine.sh) and ended by rc=.
set -u
PROGS="explorations/run-c4/src/MicroGptFlatQuick.fss explorations/apl/mg/MicroGptAplQuick.fss"; LIMIT=600; A=()
for a in "$@"; do
  if [ "$a" = full ]; then PROGS="explorations/run-c4/src/MicroGptFlatCheck.fss explorations/apl/mg/MicroGptAplCheck.fss"; LIMIT=5400
  else A+=("$a"); fi
done
set -- "${A[@]}"
cd "$(dirname "$0")/../../.."                               # $FORTRESS_HOME
- P-29 **Walk's speed is irrelevant to every judgement of Fortress's performance.** Walk is far slower than Python's interpreter (`explorations/microgpt-port.md`, "Step-0 results", a measurement of 2026-08-23). Fortress's performance is judged on the compiled path, once the compiler runs programs. So no performance decision rests on walk's timings. In particular, until microGPT runs compiled, C4, the flat microGPT program, is not edited for speed. The gate never runs microGPT's two programs, C4 and the APL-style program, because they run too long to be tests. Why: walk is the unoptimised path, as a debug build is in Swift, where performance is not judged either.

## Gate

One run on the merged tree, its logs under `tmp/gate-batch-<N>/`, its three outputs written by fixed functions, never by hand. The functions of steps 5 and 7 (`gate_summary`, `gate_compare`, `last_landed_summary`, `ladder_filter`, `ladder_compare`, `mg_phases`) are in `tools/gate-functions.sh`, which the gate sources from the tree's root with `FORTRESS_HOME` set; until 2026-10-10 they were strings of the script (`reviews/skills-agenda-audit.md`, finding GA2). Its steps:

1. The disk.
2. `rm -rf ProjectFortress/TEST-RESULTS`, then `ant compileAll`, and at once the distance stage started in the background.
3. The library order if the build started the caches again, then two copies of the caches for the ladder.
4. `ant testFast`, then `ant testSystem`, never both at once, at four threads, pinned in `build.xml` (P-125, "The suites run Fortress in parallel."). Then `ant testSpecData` once an approved rung brings it into the gate, or the last landed summary has a `specdata/` row; every example must pass (P-124, "The specification's examples join the gate at zero red.").
5. `summary.txt` from `gate_summary`, one row per suite read from the plain-formatter files under `TEST-RESULTS/`, because the parallel tracks interleave their lines in the ant log. It ends with the `BUILD` and `Total time` lines and the machine it ran on (`# machine `, from `rung-flat-tower/machine.sh`), so that timings are read against their machine. `gate_compare` against the newest landed summary: a failure, an empty suite, a count that fell or a suite gone is red. The `system-<i>` shards are compared by their sum, since `testSystem` is one suite sharded by sorted index and a new file moves every later file along the shards; climb batch 2's gate went red on exactly that (`compile-ladder/climb-batch-2/JUDGE-gate.md`).
6. The four-thread atomic runs: 14 programs, three runs each, 42 lines. A FAIL, NO-PASS or compile failure is red; a timeout is re-run once.
7. The ladder regression (the skill's `gate.md`): the 85 files of the baseline's pass list compared on phase and output, the `Operation took` line masked, and the eighteen microGPT components compiled only. A DOWN, STDOUT or MISSING line is red unless a rung declared it.
8. The checker count, and 9. the distance, below.

A red gate goes to a judge, then one repair, then one more gate. A gate red after its repair stops the batch, nothing pushed.

### The checker count, and a rung whose test is that stage

The gate's step 8 runs the compiler's checker over the interpreter's library (`tools/checker-count/run.sh`, about 5 minutes since climb batch 13b: 387 s in 13b's gate, 303 s on batch 14's rung L's tree and under 5 minutes in its gate, against the stage's 900 s limit) and compares its total with the last landed one. That can run past the Bash tool's 300 s limit, so a rung's worker starts the stage detached with nohup and waits for it with `wait_for`, as the skill's `session.md`, "Long commands", gives them; the distance stage below runs the same way, about half an hour (26 to 29 minutes in batch 14). It answers the library route: one library, the interpreter's, becomes the library the compiler checks (P-37, "The library route."). The total is reported and never red (P-39, "The checker count is measured, never red."). A fix can raise it, because the checker stops checking an api at its first errors, and two rungs' changes do not add. `checker_compare` is red only on a crash line no rung declared, a stale shadow (the instrumented copy no longer matching the tracked checker), or a table with no total. The overloading checker's memo is off in the stage, since it hides 27 to 35 errors depending on build order.

A `testIsStage` rung has that stage as its test: its before is the last landed table, run once after the edit and rebuild. No program can yet be compiled against the interpreter's library, so this is the one place a permanent stage stands in for a test file.

A rung whose every path lies under `explorations/`, `Specification/`, `Documentation/`, a test corpus, the test harness's sources, or walk's evaluator and natives runs neither stage. Both stages run only the compiler's phases (F-111, "The checker-count and distance stages read only the compiler's phases ..."; `STAGE_BLIND`).

### The distance stage

The full measurement of the distance to the switch-over, reported and never red (P-39, "The checker count is measured, never red."). `tools/distance/run.sh` runs every stage of the checker over the twelve prelude components in one JVM, under shadows made from the tracked sources at each run, with the compiled path's setting and the implicit bound `Any`. An edit that no longer matches stops the run, and `#shadow` says STALE. It starts beside the suites right after `compileAll` and is read last; `compare.sh` prints DISTANCE DOWN, UP or SAME and what moved, and always exits 0. The commit stage lands `distance.txt` and the per-site list, `explorations/compile-ladder/gate/distance-sites.tsv`, which the next batch's rungs read as their before.

160:- F-141 **Under `walk`, a type parameter that nothing at a call fixes takes its declared bound, and a lone one with no narrowest candidate takes its bound where every argument is below it.** It builds P-48. A lone type parameter is one that is the whole declared type of some argument and that no other argument fixes (F-137); where some argument is not below its bound, it takes the arguments' join. A type parameter that the declared parameter types mention only in function domains, an odd number of arrows deep and never inside a static argument, as `T` in `g: T -> ZZ32`, is bounded by the arguments only from above. Where nothing bounds it from below, it takes the meet of its declared bound and the bounds that the arguments place on it. An F-bounded parameter stays open (F-143). A reduction or comprehension that writes no static argument fixes its big operator's parameter by the declared type of its value, else by its elements' join (F-228). That rule is the coordinator's call. Two more rules are defaults of the walk-instance rung's decision record. First, a parameter that only another fixed parameter's bound mentions takes that parameter's instance, not its own bound: `ap[\T, A extends T\](a: A)` gives `T` the type of `a` (D3, row 592). Second, a lone one whose bound mentions a static parameter has the arguments' supertypes among its candidates, and so takes their narrowest common supertype, never its bound (D5). Defects, each with an expected failure: two bounds that walk cannot meet (row 591); a bound only from above that mentions another static parameter, which keeps `Bottom` (walk's `BottomType`) (row 612); two upper bounds from two function arguments that walk cannot meet, which fail the call (row 616); a parameter that only the result of a function expression with no declared return type fixes, which takes `Bottom` (row 587); a generic passed over at dispatch when its arguments have several minimal common supertypes (row 589), whose repair changes which declaration runs, the curator's to decide. A type parameter that a parameter's declared type mentions inside another type, as `List[\T\]` mentions `T`, is fixed by the argument at that position. One that is the whole declared type of one or more parameters, as `T` is of `x: T`, and that nothing else fixes, takes the narrowest type, within its bounds, that every one of those arguments has or converts into: `ZZ64` for a `ZZ32` and an `NN32`. Where there is none, and no numeral settles the tie, it takes its bound, narrowed by what the call's expected type requires of the return type (P-48). The source is [Proof of Overloading Resolution for Functions](../../Specification/appendices/overloading-function.tex),
especially `lem:subset`, `lem:le`, `thm:overloading-subtyping` and
`thm:dynamic-subtype-static`. Keep its finite-candidate argument, for
calls applicable **without coercion**. Here declarations have ground domain
and return types; an intermediate argument type such as `G[\ZZ32\]`
is ground too. Assume the existing no-duplicates rule, concrete implementation
availability, body typing, and a sound, transitive subtype relation.
Equivalent domains are identified for ordering purposes.

This does not prove the lift to quantified generic overloads or inference:
their instantiation and Return Type Rule obligations remain with batch 7b.
[Welterweight](../../Papers/Welterweight/evaluation.tick) supplies the useful
notion of a value's *ilk* (its most specific runtime type), but explicitly
says its broader propositions are not rigorously proved. This note does not
measured here. It is not, by itself, evidence of an unsafe value conversion.

**Brief amendment for C:** use a coverage query local to overload validity
(and the static-tie justification), reusing clause/exclusion helpers as
appropriate. Do not broaden the shared normalizer merely because the old
one contains a related rule. Preserve existing general subtype verdicts in
this rung; repairing their overall consistency is separate work. The
existing `SkBetweenAssign` guard alone cannot detect every change involving
an explicitly written intersection or union. Any proposed global change
must have its assignment/equivalence consequences reviewed explicitly.

applicable to a dynamic call is the same as or more specific than every
declaration that is applicable to the corresponding static call, so that, by

declaration is more specific than, and every declaration more specific than them

the intersection of their return types; where there is one such declaration,
that is its return type.

For integer results, division by zero throws a \TYP{DivisionByZero}.
For rational results, division by zero produces \EXP{1/0}.
For floating-point results, division by zero produces a \TYP{NaN} value
according to the rules of IEEE 754.
For intervals, division by zero produces an appropriate containing interval
(which under many circumstances will be the interval of all possible real values and infinities).

Wraparound multiplication on fixed-size integers is expressed by
\EXP{\dottimes}.
Saturating multiplication on fixed-size integers is expressed by
\EXP{\boxdot} or \EXP{\boxtimes}.
These operations do not overflow.

Ordinary multiplication and division of floating-point numbers always
use the IEEE 754 ``round to nearest'' rounding mode.  This rounding
mode may be emphasized by using the operators \EXP{\otimes} (or \EXP{\odot})
and \EXP{\oslash}.  Multiplication and division in ``round toward zero''
mode may be expressed with \EXP{\boxtimes} (or \EXP{\boxdot}) and
\EXP{\boxslash}.
Multiplication and division in ``round toward positive infinity''
mode may be expressed with \EXP{\uptimes} (or \EXP{\updot}) and \EXP{\upslash}.
Multiplication and division in ``round toward negative infinity''
mode may be expressed with \EXP{\downtimes} (or \EXP{\downdot}) and
\EXP{\downslash}.

\subsection{Addition and Subtraction Operators}

Addition and subtraction are expressed with \EXP{+} and \EXP{-} on all numeric quantities,
including intervals, as well as vectors and matrices.

The handling of overflow depends on the type of the number produced.
For integer results, overflow throws an \TYP{IntegerOverflow}.
Rational computations do not overflow.
For floating-point results, overflow produces \EXP{+\infty} or \EXP{-\infty}
according to the rules of IEEE 754.
For intervals, overflow produces an appropriate containing interval.

Underflow is relevant only to floating-point computations and is handled
according to the rules of IEEE 754.

Wraparound addition and subtraction on fixed-size integers are
expressed by \EXP{\dotplus} and \EXP{\dotminus}.
Saturating addition and subtraction on fixed-size integers are
expressed by \EXP{\boxplus} and \EXP{\boxminus}.
These operations do not overflow.

This is what the type system promises: a diagonal is a kind of matrix, with a faster product of its own. Gap-ledger row 299 records what the general product costs on a diagonal: 13 to 54 times as much as scaling the rows. Built: the six operators left to the library, and `Diag`'s `mul`. It states instead the overloading model of the type group's 2011 paper (`Papers/Types/`), which the compiled checker already used. The checker keeps the paper's three rules: No Duplicates, Meet and Return Type. It checks the Return Type Rule over every instance of a generic declaration that the argument types allow, not over one guessed instance. One rule of the old sentence survives: if one generic declaration is more specific than another, their static parameters must line up position by position, as Java's rule for overriding a generic method requires. The compiled checker enforces it (F-75 gives its form and scope). Walk chooses among overloads by the parameter types that each declaration declares, not by the order in which they are written. At load, walk judges each pair of two generic declarations by the checker's rules on their declared parameter types. It does not refuse a pair only because none of their parameter types exclude, as when one declaration is more specific than the other. Walk and the checker must accept the same pairs. The library repairs, by declarations of its own, the overload sets that the checker refused, and no line of microGPT's two programs changes. Where walk or the checker still judges a pair against these rules: walk compares two functional methods of a generic trait or object on the instance that a call makes (F-26); both paths refuse the paper's own valid example (row 539); walk refuses two generic functional methods of a trait without static parameters whose declared domains lie one inside the other, and fails at a call on such a pair in a generic trait (rows 779 and 780); and walk and the checker disagree on four kinds of pair (rows 759 and 786 to 788).

A generic declaration applies if some type within its bounds takes the arguments. Only then is the chosen declaration instantiated by promotion: at the narrowest type into which its arguments coerce (P-74). So beside `op(a: Any, b: Any)`, `op[\T extends Number\](a: T, b: T)` applies to a call with a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64`, at `T = Number`. It is the more specific, so it runs, at `ZZ64`. Its instance is then the intersection of its upper bounds (`Any` if it has none). At checking, that is narrowed by what the call's expected type (P-49 defines it) requires of the declared return type; at run time, by the static type that the checker gave the call. It is never `Bottom`, never the union of the arguments' types, and never the value's type alone. The rule sets the instance, not which declaration runs (P-46). Why: the rule is the team's later word, from the POPL 2019 paper on multiple dispatch, and the curator trusts the team's later work above his own understanding (P-26).
